content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Explain what indicators are and how they work
Describe common indicators and their colour changes
Choose appropriate indicators for different purposes
Explain the difference between indicators and universal indicator
are substances that change colour depending on whether they are in an acidic or alkaline solution. They are essential tools for determining the pH of solutions and for titrations.
A substance that has different colours in acidic and alkaline solutions.
Indicators are weak acids or bases themselves
They have different colours in their acidic and basic forms
The colour change occurs at a specific pH range
Only shows acid or alkali (not pH)
Good for strong acid/strong base titrations
Colourless in acid and neutral solutions
Only turns pink in alkaline solutions
is a mixture of several indicators that shows a range of colours for different pH values.
[DIAGRAM: pH colour chart showing colour gradient from red through orange, yellow, green, blue to purple]
Shows approximate pH, not just acid/alkali
Use universal indicator to find approximate pH
Or use litmus for simple acid/alkali test
Red in acid → purple neutral → blue/green in alkali
One of the best natural indicators
Shows many different colours at different pH values
Can be made by boiling red cabbage in water
A student adds litmus to solution A, which turns red. They add litmus to solution B, which turns blue. What can they conclude?
Solution A turned litmus red, so it is
Solution B turned litmus blue, so it is
Litmus only tells us if a solution is acidic or alkaline
It doesn't tell us the exact pH
Explain why phenolphthalein would not be a suitable indicator for a titration between hydrochloric acid and ammonia solution (a weak alkali).
When neutralised by a strong acid, the endpoint pH is below 7
At the endpoint, the solution would still be colourless
The colour change would occur too late (after the endpoint)
Methyl orange (changes at pH 3.5-4.5) would be more suitable
A solution is tested with universal indicator and gives a yellow colour. What is the approximate pH? Is the solution acidic, neutral, or alkaline?
It is a weak acid (not strongly acidic like pH 1-2)
Describe how you would make an indicator from red cabbage.
Chop red cabbage into small pieces
Place in a beaker and add just enough water to cover
Heat gently (or boil) for about 10 minutes
The water turns purple/blue as the indicator dissolves
Strain the liquid to remove cabbage pieces
The purple liquid can now be used as an indicator
It will turn red/pink in acids and blue/green in alkalis
Thinking all indicators show different colours for different pH values
Simple indicators like litmus only show acid vs alkali; you need universal indicator for pH range
Use single indicators (methyl orange, phenolphthalein) for titrations - clearer endpoint
Thinking phenolphthalein is pink in neutral solutions
Phenolphthalein is COLOURLESS in both acidic AND neutral solutions
change colour in acids and alkalis
Red in acid, blue in alkali (simple test)
Red in acid, yellow in alkali (changes at low pH)
Colourless in acid, pink in alkali (changes at high pH)
Shows range of colours for different pH values
can be extracted from coloured plants
